title_eng: Toward Objectification of Subjective Chronic Pain Based on Implicit Response in Biosignals
abstract:
Abstract— Objective: Chronic pain necessitates early 
intervention and accurate evaluation. Current subjective 
questionnaire -based methods have limitations. This study aims to 
develop a chronic pain assessment method based on multi -modal 
biosignal and to validate its feasibility. Methods: We present a 
model utilizing electroencephalogram (EEG), photoplethysmo - 
gram (PPG), electrocardiogram (ECG), and facial temperature 
(FT) data from 59 subjects (26 chronic pain patients). A total of 
112 features were derived from all signals, and 17 of them showed 
a significant difference between the chronic pains and the normal 
control. Results: By optimizing signal types and feature 
combinations, our pain classification model significantly 
enhanced chronic pain assessment (AUROC: 0.802 to 0.864). 
Notable features included PPG systolic length (12.3%), EEG 
alpha band power (11.1%), and delta band power (9.4%). 
Conclusion: This multi-modal biosignal approach holds promise 
for effective chronic pain quantification. 
Index Terms— Chronic pain assessment, electroencephalogram, 
photoplethysmogram, electrocardiogram, facial temperature. 
I. INTRODUCTION 
HORNIC PAIN is a different disease from acute pain, 
referring to pain that persists or recurs for months or years, 
even after the damaged tissue has been recovered [1, 2] . For 
proper management of chronic pain, early diagnosis of the type 
and cause of pain is essential, however, in most cases, it is 
difficult because the patient usually visits the hospital after the 
symptoms have worsened. Delays in the diagnosis and 
treatment of chronic pain can reduce treatment effectiveness, 
lead to long -term health issues, and diminish the patient’s 
quality of life. Consequently, the effective detection and 
management of chronic pain holds importance and the demand 
for objective assessment methods continues to escalate.

questionnaires that evaluate the pain level using a score [3, 4]. 
The questionnaire -based chronic pain assessment technique 
refers to a method in which the patient expresses their own 
current pain state and has a drawback in that it is subjective and 
varies significantly depending on the patient’s individual 
characteristics. Although various questionnaire methods have 
been proposed to improve accuracy and subjectivity [5, 6], it is 
still necessary to develop an objective evaluation technique for 
chronic pain. 
This study performs a quantitative assessment of chronic 
pain and validates the potential of a sophisticated chronic pain 
assessment technique. Notably, we used a multi -modal 
approach, which is rarely addressed in the existing literature. 
The multimodal approach is expected to provide a more 
comprehensive and accurate assessment by integrating 
different biosignals. We acquired information on the 
electrocardiogram ( ECG), photoplethysmogram ( PPG), 
electroencephalogram ( EEG), and facial temperature (FT) of 
chronic pain patients and normal groups through clinical trials; 
and developed a model to evaluate the presence or absence of 
chronic pain by extracting and combining the characteristic 
features for each signal, and subsequently verified the model’s 
performance. 
II. RELATED WORKS 
As a method for the early diagnosis and objectification of the 
degree of chronic pain, chronic pain evaluation methods using 
various bio -signals such as ECG, PPG, EEG, and body 
temperature have been proposed [7 -23]. The heart rate 
variability (HRV) is mainly used to observe autonomic changes 
using an ECG [7]. In a chronic pain study using HRV, a 
consistent decrease in the HRV under high frequency (HF) 
power [8], and in the root-mean-square of successive difference 
(RMSSD) [9], due to changes in the parasympathetic nerve 
activity, were reported in the chronic pain group. Additionally, 
in patients with chronic neuropathic pain, a positive correlation 
between the analgesic efficacy and ratio of the low frequency 
power to the high frequency power (LF/HF), was reported [10]. 
Furthermore, while evaluating chronic fibromyalgia, it was 
shown that the total power (TP) related to the overall autonomic 
nerve activity, and the RMSSD related to parasympathetic 
nerve activity, have the potential to be used as useful markers 
for chronic pain [11]. The PPG, a technique for the 
non-invasive measurement of the changes in the local blood 
volume, is frequently used in pain research because it reflects

the autonomic activity expressed in the vasomotor tone and 
pulse rate changes [2, 12]. For a pulse rate variability (PRV) 
induced in a PPG in a similar manner to the HRV, significant 
changes in the heart rate interval, heart rate, HF, LF, and LF/HF 
were observed before and after myofascial pain treatment [13]. 
The surgical pleth index, a commercialized index to evaluate 
surgical pain based on the amplitude or PPG pulse -to-pulse 
interval, was reported to have a significant difference before 
and after chronic pain treatment [13]. In addition, studies have 
been conducted to evaluate pain and analgesic efficacy using an 
electroencephalogram (EEG) [14, 15]. In a study analyzing the 
EEG of chronic pain patients, an increase in the theta and alpha 
band powers was reported in the chronic pain group [16-18], 
and a decrease in the amplitude of the evoked potentials [19, 20] 
was observed as the duration of pain increased. Additionally, 
pain can cause changes in the body temperature. In the case of 
inflammatory pain, an increase in the temperature at the 
inflammation site, and a decrease in the skin temperature at the 
pain site, was reported in the fibromyalgia syndrome case 
[21-23]. In addition, it has been reported that there is a 
possibility of an increase in the body temperature in cases of 
chronic pain accompanied by infection [21, 22]. The results of 
the above studies suggest that various bio -signals have the 
potential to be used in chronic pain assessment. However, a 
reliable chronic pain objectification technique that can be 
universally applied regardless of the cause has not yet been 
developed. Moreover, previous studies [7-23] have primarily 
utilized a unimodality to observe changes in specific chronic 
pain. It is known that a multi -modal approach to understand 
human body phenomena by combining various bio -signals can 
present multi -faceted information on human physiology, 
thereby providing more sophisticated and accurate progress. 
III. MATERIALS AND METHODS 
The overall process used in this study is shown in Fig. 1. 
Multi-modal biosignals from the chronic pain and normal 
control groups were recorded, and the features were extracted 
through the pre -processing of each signal. Subsequently, a 
classification model based on multivariate logistic regression 
was developed by combining the extracted features, and the 
feature set was optimized using the sequential forward search 
algorithm [24] that searches for the optimal feature set by 
adding the most effective features based on the performance 
evaluation metric. In this study, MATLAB 2020a (Mathworks, 
Natick, MA, USA) was used in the pre -processing and feature 
extraction of the acquired information on the EEG, ECG, PPG, 
and FT; and the CURRY8 (Compumedics, El Paso, TX, USA) 
software was used for EEG signal-processing. 
A. Experimental Protocol Setup and Multi-Modal Signal Data 
Acquisition 
Before the commencement of data acquisition, participants 
with factors that can induce changes in the autonomic nerve 
activity, such as those with cardiovascular diseases, those 
taking autonomic modulation drugs such as antidepressants, 
those who had insufficient sleep, those who consumed caffeine 
or smoked within 2 hours of the experiment, and those who 
exercised vigorously, were excluded through screening. Prior 
to data acquisition, participants reported their current severity 
of pain using a 10-point visual analogue scale (VAS, 0: no pain, 
10: severe pain). Subsequently, in the sitting position, we 
measured ECG, PPG, EEG, and facial temperature 
simultaneously for 6 minutes. The ECG and EEG were 
recorded at 2,048 Hz using a ActiveTwo (Biosemi., AMS,
